note: Declarative list of what macro.py fetches. Each series: id, source (adapter), source_id, name and one-line 'what', unit, freq (D/W/M/Q/A), kind (index: % changes; count: level changes; rate: percentage-point changes; flow: monthly flows summed over 12 months), release, group, store (false = third-party copyright: never fetched into this public repo), priority, licence, revised, stale_after_days (backstop when the release calendar does not cover the series). Views carry their fixed thresholds here so a reader can see them.

trend_rule: Trend leg (the board's one definition, regime_core / regime.py): +1 when the series is above a rising 50-session exponential average (rising = higher than 21 sessions earlier), -1 when below a falling one, 0 otherwise.

side_rule.text: Each test sits WITH the view when its value is beyond the 'confirm' threshold, AGAINST it when beyond the 'refute' threshold, and NEITHER in between. With c tests with and r against: c - r >= 2 is 'with'; c - r = 1 is 'leaning with'; c = r (both above zero) is 'mixed'; no test past either threshold is 'neutral'; r - c = 1 is 'leaning against'; r - c >= 2 is 'against'. Fewer than half the tests with data is 'not enough data'.

codes.with: The data sit with this view
codes.lean_with: The data lean toward this view
codes.mixed: The data are split on this view
codes.neutral: The data sit between the thresholds on this view
codes.lean_against: The data lean against this view
codes.against: The data sit against this view
codes.insufficient: Not enough data to place this view

reads.title: Labour-market temperature
reads.formula: Mean of five robust z-scores, each against its own trailing 10 years (median and 1.4826 x median absolute deviation, so 2020 does not swamp the scale), signed so positive means tighter: minus the 3-month change in the unemployment rate; minus initial claims' 4-week average against its own 52-week average (%); the 3-month average payroll change; the quits rate; job openings per unemployed person. Shown with the Sahm gap: 3-month average unemployment rate minus its lowest 3-month average of the prior 12 months.
reads.limits: The October 2025 household-survey gap blanks 3-month averages that span it. The payroll pace that keeps unemployment steady is uncertain while immigration shifts labour supply, so payroll change is read against its own history, not a fixed neutral number. The Sahm gap's 0.5 pp line marked the start of every US recession since 1970 and triggered in August 2024 without one.

reads.title: Wages against productivity and prices
reads.formula: Employment Cost Index wages, year over year, minus labour productivity, year over year (4-quarter changes); compared with core PCE prices, year over year.
reads.limits: Arithmetic identity (wage growth minus productivity growth is unit-labour-cost growth); no track record claimed. Productivity is noisy quarter to quarter.

reads.title: Breadth of inflation
reads.formula: Three gaps: median CPI minus headline CPI, and trimmed-mean CPI minus headline CPI (each the 3-month average of the monthly annual rate against headline's 3-month annualised change); sticky-price core minus flexible-price CPI, year over year.
reads.limits: The share of the ~70 CPI categories rising faster than 3% needs the BLS key (not created yet), so only the three gaps are shown.

reads.title: Fed reaction: policy rate, rule and market path
reads.formula: Policy-range midpoint; the Atlanta Fed Taylor-rule utility's FOMCTaylor99UR prescription; the fed funds futures strip's implied rate for the next policy month and about 6 and 12 months out (100 minus price); the latest FOMC median projections. Value: the change the futures price over about 12 months (pp).
reads.limits: The neutral rate inside any Taylor rule is disputed; the utility shows one documented choice. Futures embed a term premium, so they are not a pure expectation.

reads.title: Fiscal impulse
reads.formula: 12-month primary deficit (deficit excluding interest on the public debt) as a share of nominal GDP, now minus 12 months earlier, in percentage points; positive means fiscal policy is putting more into demand than a year ago. Tariff refunds are shown as a separate line.
reads.limits: Payment-timing shifts move single months, so only 12-month sums are used. A tariff refund is a one-off transfer to importers, not a policy stance. The Brookings Hutchins Fiscal Impact Measure is the published comparator (availability not established).

reads.title: Small against large businesses
reads.formula: Rows, each small minus large where a pair exists: banks tightening to small firms minus to large and mid firms (net %); business applications, year over year; trend of the small-cap to large-cap price ratio (IWM / SPY) and of small to mid (IJR / IJH), by the board's trend-leg rule.
reads.limits: ADP payrolls by firm size are third-party copyright and are not published here, so the payroll row is missing in v1.

reads.title: Dollar, emerging markets and Europe: the relative cycle
reads.formula: Broad dollar, year over year; BIS real effective dollar, year over year; 2-year Treasury yield minus the euro overnight rate (pp); OECD leading indicators for the US, Germany and China; trend legs for EEM / SPY, VGK / SPY, EMLC and CEW.
reads.limits: Leading indicators are revised heavily; compare levels across countries at one vintage. No track record claimed.

reads.title: Capital spending as an inflation input
reads.formula: 3-month annualised growth of data-centre construction, core capital-goods orders and transformer prices, beside electricity prices and construction wages, year over year.
reads.limits: Census construction data are revised in place with no vintages. No track record claimed.

series.name: Consumer prices (CPI)
series.what: The consumer price index for all urban consumers (CPI-U): the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services that households in US cities pay for, seasonally adjusted (index, 1982-84 = 100), published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It is the headline US inflation figure. The Fed's 2% goal is set on PCE prices instead, which usually run a few tenths of a point below CPI because they weight the basket differently and cover more.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Core consumer prices
series.what: Core CPI: the consumer price index for all urban consumers excluding food and energy, seasonally adjusted, published monthly by BLS. Food and fuel prices swing with harvests and oil, so leaving them out gives a steadier read of the underlying trend that interest rates can influence. Read the 3-month pace at an annual rate for the recent trend and the year-over-year change for the level against the 2% goal.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Shelter prices
series.what: CPI shelter: the cost of housing services, made up mainly of rent of a primary residence, owners' equivalent rent and lodging away from home, seasonally adjusted, BLS. It is about a third of the CPI basket and moves slowly, because each sampled home is priced only every six months and most leases reset once a year, so it trails market rents by about a year. A 3-month annual rate below the year-over-year rate means shelter inflation is slowing.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Owners' equivalent rent
series.what: Owners' equivalent rent of primary residence (OER): the CPI's estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their own homes, worked out by BLS from the rents of comparable rented homes, seasonally adjusted. It is the largest single CPI item, about a quarter of the basket, and it tracks rents, not house prices or mortgage rates. Because it follows leases as they renew, it trails new-lease market rents by about a year.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Core goods prices
series.what: CPI core goods (commodities less food and energy commodities): prices of physical goods other than food and fuel, such as cars, clothing, furniture and appliances, seasonally adjusted, BLS. Before 2020 these prices tended to drift down slowly. A rising rate points to tariffs or supply costs passing through to shoppers, and it is the first place a tariff increase shows up in consumer prices.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Core services prices
series.what: CPI core services (services less energy services): prices of services other than electricity and piped gas, such as rent, medical care, insurance, transport and recreation, seasonally adjusted, BLS. It is about 60% of the CPI basket and is driven largely by housing and labour costs, so it changes slowly. A high 3-month rate here is the main reason core inflation stays above the 2% goal.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Services prices excluding shelter
series.what: CPI services less rent of shelter: all CPI services other than rent, owners' equivalent rent and lodging, seasonally adjusted, BLS. It still includes energy services such as electricity, so it is close to, but not the same as, the core-services-excluding-housing measure Fed officials discuss. These prices depend most on wages, so a high rate here means labour costs are feeding inflation.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Consumer spending prices (PCE)
series.what: The price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE): prices of everything households consume, including spending made on their behalf such as employer-paid health insurance (index, 2017 = 100, seasonally adjusted). Published monthly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in its Personal Income and Outlays release, about two weeks after CPI. Its change from a year earlier is the measure the Fed's 2% inflation goal is defined on.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Core PCE prices
series.what: Core PCE prices: the PCE price index excluding food and energy, seasonally adjusted, published monthly by BEA. The Fed's 2% goal is defined on headline PCE, but the FOMC treats core PCE as the better guide to where inflation is heading and projects it in its Summary of Economic Projections. A year-over-year figure above 2% means underlying inflation is running above the goal.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Median CPI (Cleveland Fed)
series.what: Median CPI, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland: each month the CPI components are ranked by price change, and the change of the component in the middle of the spending-weighted ranking is taken, shown as a one-month change at an annual rate (seasonally adjusted). Because it ignores the largest rises and falls, it shows what the typical price is doing. Median CPI above headline means inflation is broad; below it means a few large movers are carrying the headline.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Trimmed-mean CPI (Cleveland Fed)
series.what: The 16% trimmed-mean CPI, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland: the spending-weighted average of CPI component price changes after dropping the components in the top 8% and bottom 8% of the ranking, shown as a one-month change at an annual rate. Cutting both tails removes one-off swings, such as a jump in airfares, and leaves the underlying trend. Read it beside median CPI: both well below headline means outliers are driving the headline.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Trimmed-mean PCE (Dallas Fed)
series.what: The trimmed-mean PCE inflation rate, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas: each month the price changes of the individual PCE components are ranked, 24% of the spending weight is cut from the bottom and 31% from the top, and the rest is averaged by weight; this is the change over 12 months. It filters unusual price moves out of the PCE measure the Fed's goal is set on. A reading near 2% means underlying PCE inflation is close to the goal.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Sticky-price core CPI (Atlanta Fed)
series.what: Sticky-price core CPI, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta: the change from a year earlier in the core CPI items (excluding food and energy) whose prices are reset relatively rarely. Prices that change rarely tend to build in expected future inflation when they are set, so this measure moves slowly and shows the persistent part of inflation. Compare it with flexible-price CPI: sticky running above flexible means inflation is embedded rather than passing.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Flexible-price CPI (Atlanta Fed)
series.what: Flexible-price CPI, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta: the change from a year earlier in the CPI items whose prices are reset often, food and energy included. These prices react quickly to demand, supply shocks and commodity prices, so the measure is volatile and shows current pressure rather than the lasting trend. Flexible running well above sticky points to a fast, possibly passing impulse such as an oil shock.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Producer prices, final demand
series.what: The producer price index for final demand: prices domestic producers receive for goods, services and construction sold to final users, seasonally adjusted (index, November 2009 = 100), published monthly by BLS. It measures prices at the producer's gate, so it shows cost pressure before it reaches shops. Several of its parts, such as medical care and airfares, feed directly into the PCE price index.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Import prices
series.what: The import price index for all commodities: prices of goods brought into the US, measured by BLS in dollars before any duties are paid, not seasonally adjusted (index, 2000 = 100), monthly. Because duties are left out, a rise here means foreign sellers or a weaker dollar are raising prices. A flat reading while tariffs rise means the duty is being paid on the US side, by importers or their customers.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 5-year breakeven inflation
series.what: The 5-year breakeven inflation rate: the 5-year Treasury yield minus the 5-year Treasury inflation-protected (TIPS) yield, both at constant maturity, computed daily by the St. Louis Fed's FRED from Treasury data. It is the average yearly CPI inflation at which the two bonds would pay the same, so it is the market's inflation compensation for the next five years. It carries a risk premium and a TIPS liquidity effect, so it is not a pure forecast; about 2.3-2.5% has usually been read as consistent with 2% PCE inflation.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 10-year breakeven inflation
series.what: The 10-year breakeven inflation rate: the 10-year Treasury yield minus the 10-year TIPS yield, both at constant maturity, computed daily by the St. Louis Fed's FRED from Treasury data. It is the market's average yearly CPI inflation compensation over the next decade, including risk and liquidity premiums. It moves less than the 5-year rate on oil shocks, so a rise here says more about long-run inflation worries.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 5-year inflation compensation, 5 years ahead
series.what: The 5-year, 5-year forward inflation rate (5y5y): the average yearly inflation the bond market prices for the five years that begin five years from now, worked out by FRED from the 5- and 10-year Treasury and TIPS yields. By looking past near-term shocks it is the market gauge Fed officials watch for whether long-run expectations stay anchored. A sustained move well above about 2.5% would mean markets doubt the 2% goal.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 1-year expected inflation (Cleveland Fed model)
series.what: Expected inflation over the next 12 months from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's model, monthly. The model combines Treasury yields, inflation data, inflation swaps and surveys of inflation expectations, and separates expected inflation from the risk premiums inside bond yields. It is a smoother, model-based alternative to raw breakevens; a reading above 3% means near-term expectations sit well above the 2% goal.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Household 1-year inflation expectations (Michigan survey)
series.what: The median price change US households expect over the next 12 months, from the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, monthly. Household expectations matter because they feed into wage demands and spending, and they react strongly to gasoline and food prices. Not shown on the board: the series is third-party copyright and is not published from the public data repository.
series.licence: University of Michigan: third-party copyright; display only, never stored in the public repo

series.source_id: nowcast_month.json, last chart block, series 'CPI Inflation'
series.name: Nowcast of this month's CPI change (Cleveland Fed)
series.what: The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's estimate of this month's headline CPI change before BLS publishes it, as a month-over-month percent change (not at an annual rate). The model uses daily oil prices, weekly retail gasoline prices, food prices and past CPI and PCE readings, and is refreshed each business day. It is most useful for energy-driven headline moves; 0.17% a month is roughly 2% a year.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.source_id: nowcast_month.json, last chart block, series 'Core CPI Inflation'

series.what: The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's estimate of this month's core CPI change (excluding food and energy) before BLS publishes it, month over month and not at an annual rate, refreshed each business day. For core prices the model leans mainly on past core readings, so it extends the recent trend rather than spotting turns. About 0.17% a month is roughly 2% a year.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.what: The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's estimate of this month's headline PCE price change before BEA publishes it, month over month and not at an annual rate. The model uses daily oil prices, weekly gasoline prices, food prices and past CPI and PCE readings, and is refreshed each business day. PCE is the measure the Fed's 2% goal is set on; about 0.17% a month is roughly 2% a year.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.source_id: nowcast_month.json, last chart block, series 'Core PCE Inflation'
series.name: Nowcast of this month's core PCE change (Cleveland Fed)
series.what: The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's estimate of this month's core PCE price change (excluding food and energy) before BEA publishes it, month over month and not at an annual rate, refreshed each business day. It leans mainly on past core readings, and once CPI and PPI for the month are out it mostly reflects how they map into PCE. About 0.17% a month is roughly 2% a year.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution

series.name: Fed funds policy range, top
series.what: The top of the federal funds policy range set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), daily (Federal Reserve Board via FRED). The Fed sets a range a quarter point wide for the overnight rate banks charge each other and steers the market rate into it with the interest it pays on reserves and its reverse-repo rate. A change in this figure is a change in monetary policy.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Fed funds policy range, bottom
series.what: The bottom of the federal funds policy range set by the FOMC, daily (Federal Reserve Board via FRED). It is also the rate the Fed pays at its overnight reverse-repo facility, so it acts as a floor for overnight money-market rates. The policy range moves only at FOMC decisions, normally in steps of a quarter point.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Effective fed funds rate
series.what: The effective federal funds rate: the volume-weighted median rate on overnight unsecured loans of reserves between banks and other institutions, computed daily by the New York Fed from the FR 2420 report. It is the market rate the FOMC's policy range is set for and normally sits a few hundredths of a point above the bottom of the range. A drift toward the top of the range is a sign reserves are getting scarce.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Secured overnight financing rate
series.what: The Secured Overnight Financing Rate: the volume-weighted median rate on overnight loans of cash secured by Treasury securities (repurchase agreements), published daily by the New York Fed from tri-party, GCF and centrally cleared bilateral repo trades. It replaced LIBOR as the main benchmark for dollar loans and derivatives. SOFR above the effective fed funds rate signals tight cash in funding markets, often around tax dates and Treasury settlements.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: FOMC projection of the policy rate, median
series.what: The median of FOMC participants' projections of the appropriate federal funds rate at the end of each year, from the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP, the dot plot), published at four meetings a year by the Federal Reserve Board. Each participant's dot is the midpoint of the range that person sees as appropriate; the median is not a Committee decision or a commitment. Futures above the median mean markets price a higher path than the Committee projects.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: FOMC longer-run policy rate, median
series.what: The median of FOMC participants' estimates of the federal funds rate in the longer run, once the economy is at full strength and inflation is at 2%, from the Summary of Economic Projections (Federal Reserve Board). It is the Committee's estimate of the neutral nominal rate: a policy rate above it is restrictive, below it accommodative. Subtracting 2% inflation gives the implied neutral real rate, known as r-star.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Fed balance sheet
series.what: Total assets of the Federal Reserve, Wednesday level, from the weekly H.4.1 release (millions of dollars, shown in billions). It is mostly Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities bought during quantitative easing, and it shrinks when the Fed lets maturing securities run off (quantitative tightening). A shrinking balance sheet drains reserves from the banking system and puts some upward pressure on longer yields.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Bank reserves at the Fed
series.what: Reserve balances with Federal Reserve Banks: the deposits banks keep at the Fed, as a weekly average from the H.4.1 release (shown in billions of dollars). Reserves are the banking system's cash for settling payments. When they fall too far, overnight rates rise toward the top of the policy range, as in September 2019, so the Fed ends balance-sheet runoff near the level it judges ample.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Overnight reverse repo
series.what: Cash invested overnight at the Federal Reserve's overnight reverse-repo facility (ON RRP), mainly by money market funds, in billions of dollars, daily (New York Fed via FRED). The facility pays the bottom of the policy range and soaks up surplus cash. Once it has run down near zero, further balance-sheet runoff comes out of bank reserves instead.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Financial conditions (Chicago Fed)
series.what: The Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index, weekly: a weighted average of 105 measures of risk, credit and leverage across money markets, debt and equity markets and the traditional and shadow banking systems. It is scaled so that zero is the average since 1971 and each unit is one standard deviation. Positive means tighter than average, negative looser; loose conditions support demand and can work against Fed tightening.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution
series.note: read from FRED: the Chicago Fed's own CSV stopped updating at 2026-04-24

series.name: 3-month Treasury yield
series.what: The yield on a 3-month Treasury bill at constant maturity, read from the Treasury's daily par yield curve (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED). It trades close to the policy range, so it moves mainly with the policy rate expected over the next three months. It is also what cash earns, the yardstick for longer bonds' returns.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 1-year Treasury yield
series.what: The yield on a 1-year Treasury at constant maturity, from the Treasury's daily par yield curve (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED). It reflects the policy rate the market expects over the coming year, so it rises ahead of expected rate increases. Together with the 2- and 10-year yields it lets forward rates be worked out exactly.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 2-year Treasury yield
series.what: The yield on a 2-year Treasury note at constant maturity, from the Treasury's daily par yield curve (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED). It is the point of the curve most sensitive to expected Fed policy over the next two years and moves first when markets reprice rate increases or cuts. A 2-year yield above the policy-range midpoint means the market prices rate rises ahead.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 3-year Treasury yield
series.what: The yield on a 3-year Treasury note at constant maturity, from the Treasury's daily par yield curve (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED). It reflects the expected policy path over three years plus a small term premium. Together with the 1-, 2- and 10-year yields it lets forward rates be worked out exactly.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 10-year Treasury yield
series.what: The yield on a 10-year Treasury note at constant maturity, from the Treasury's daily par yield curve (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED). It is the expected path of short rates over a decade plus a term premium, and it sets the level for mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs. It is also the main discount rate for long-lived assets, so a rise tightens financial conditions.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: Yield curve, 10-year minus 2-year
series.what: The 10-year Treasury yield minus the 2-year yield, in percentage points, daily (FRED). A negative spread, an inverted curve, means markets price lower short rates ahead, and it has come before most US recessions with long and variable lags. A spread rising back above zero often comes as the Fed starts to cut.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 10-year real yield (TIPS)
series.what: The yield on a 10-year Treasury inflation-protected security (TIPS) at constant maturity: the return above CPI inflation that is locked in for ten years (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED). It is the market's real interest rate, and a rising real yield tightens financial conditions and weighs on spending. The 10-year Treasury yield minus this figure is the 10-year breakeven inflation rate.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: 10-year term premium (Kim-Wright)
series.what: The 10-year term premium from the Kim-Wright model, published by Federal Reserve Board staff: the part of the 10-year zero-coupon Treasury yield that is extra pay for tying money up for ten years rather than rolling short bills, once the model's estimate of expected short rates is taken out. The model fits three factors to Treasury yields since 1990, so the split is an estimate and gets revised. A rising premium means investors want more for duration and inflation risk, as with large deficits.
series.licence: US federal government work: public domain

series.name: GDPNow (Atlanta Fed)
series.what: GDPNow, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta: a running model estimate of real GDP growth in the current quarter, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, re-estimated about six times a month as new data arrive. It is not an official forecast and moves with each release, and early in a quarter it can miss by a point or more. Growth well above the economy's long-run pace of about 2% keeps pressure on prices.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution
series.note: re-estimated about six times a month; the observation is dated to the quarter being estimated

series.name: Taylor-rule prescription (Atlanta Fed utility)
series.what: The policy rate a Taylor rule prescribes, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's Taylor Rule Utility, quarterly (its FOMCTaylor99UR version). It adds the neutral real rate implied by FOMC projections, the 2% goal, 1.5 times the gap between four-quarter core PCE inflation and 2%, and 1.0 times the resource gap, taken as twice the gap between the FOMC's longer-run unemployment rate and the actual rate (the 1999 weighting). It is a benchmark, not what the Fed does: a prescription well above the actual policy rate means policy is looser than this rule.
series.licence: Federal Reserve Bank research data: free, with attribution
